nameStory: Sweet-brier gets its delightful name from the sweet, apple-like fragrance that wafts from its leaves when you brush against them or crush them gently. This aromatic quality made it a favorite in old English gardens, where it was also called 'eglantine' - a romantic name that appears in Shakespeare's plays and ancient poetry.
description: Sweet-brier is a thorny shrub rose that can grow 6-10 feet tall, forming dense, arching thickets. It produces small pink flowers in early summer, followed by bright red rose hips in fall. What sets this rose apart from others is the wonderful apple-scented fragrance of its leaves, especially noticeable on humid days or when the foliage is disturbed. Originally from Europe, it has naturalized in parts of New England.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Small, compound leaves with 5-7 rounded leaflets that smell like green apples when crushed - this sweet fragrance is the plant's signature feature

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small pink flowers about 1-2 inches across with five petals and yellow centers, blooming in clusters during early summer

idTips.label: Thorns
idTips.description: Stems armed with numerous curved thorns of varying sizes - both large hooked prickles and smaller straight ones scattered along the branches

idTips.label: Fruit
idTips.description: Bright red, egg-shaped rose hips that persist into winter, about half an inch long with dried sepals still attached at the tip

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms dense, arching shrubs that can spread by suckers, often creating impenetrable thickets along roadsides and field edges

habitat: Sweet-brier thrives in sunny, well-drained locations like old fields, roadsides, pasture edges, and disturbed areas. It prefers slightly alkaline soils and is often found growing with other non-native plants in areas with past human disturbance. Look for it in abandoned farmland and along country roads where it can form substantial colonies.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge with their characteristic apple scent becoming noticeable as temperatures warm. Flower buds begin forming on previous year's growth.
seasonality.summer: Pink flowers bloom in early summer, typically June, releasing a light sweet fragrance. The aromatic leaves are at their most fragrant during warm, humid weather.
seasonality.fall: Bright red rose hips ripen and become prominent, while leaves may turn yellowish before dropping. The apple scent of bruised leaves remains strong.
seasonality.winter: Persistent red rose hips stand out against bare, thorny stems. The shrub's dense, tangled branching pattern and varied thorn sizes help with winter identification.

funFact: Sweet-brier leaves were traditionally used to scent linens and rooms - people would hang bundles of the fragrant foliage indoors as a natural air freshener, and the apple-like scent would last for weeks even after the leaves dried!
confusionNotes: Sweet-brier can be confused with other wild roses, but the apple-scented leaves are unique - no other rose in New England has this fragrance. If you're unsure, gently crush a leaf and smell it; sweet-brier's apple scent is unmistakable and immediate.
contextualKnowledge: Though called 'sweet-brier,' this plant is completely unrelated to the briers of the Smilax genus (greenbriers). The name simply refers to any thorny shrub that early settlers found growing wild, and the 'sweet' was added to distinguish this fragrant rose from other prickly plants.
compareHints: Among New England's roses, sweet-brier is the only one with apple-scented leaves - this fragrance alone separates it from multiflora rose, rugosa rose, and native species. Its small pink flowers and dense thorny growth might look similar to dog-rose, but dog-rose lacks the distinctive leaf fragrance and has different thorn patterns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England roses, multiflora rose is unique for its enormous flower clusters (other roses have flowers in smaller groups or singly) and those telltale fringed stipules.
Rugosa rose stands apart from other New England roses with its unmistakable wrinkled leaves - no other rose species has this corrugated texture.

Among New England's wild roses, swamp rose is unique in its preference for wet habitats - while Carolina rose and Virginia rose stick to drier areas, and multiflora rose (an invasive) has much denser thorns and forms larger, more aggressive colonies.
Among New England's wild roses, Carolina rose is the champion spreader, forming low colonies while relatives like swamp rose grow taller and more upright.
Among New England's wild roses, Virginian rose stands out for its glossy leaflets (rugosa rose has wrinkled leaves) and typically 7-9 leaflets per leaf (most others have fewer).

Among New England's roses, Sherard's downy-rose stands out for its compact size and distinctly grayish, downy leaves - most other wild roses like swamp rose or Carolina rose have greener, smoother foliage.

Among New England's wild roses, smooth rose is unique for its nearly thornless stems – multiflora rose has curved thorns, rugosa rose has dense straight prickles, and swamp rose has scattered thorns along its stems.
Among New England's roses, dog-rose stands out for its large, curved thorns and smooth leaflets without fuzzy coating.
Memorial rose is unique among New England roses for its prostrate, ground-hugging growth habit - all other rose species in the region grow as upright shrubs.
Among New England's wild roses, shining rose is uniquely low-growing and has by far the glossiest leaves.
Unlike the common multiflora rose with its clusters of small white flowers, cinnamon rose has larger, solitary pink blooms.
Among New England's wild roses, prickly wild rose stands out for its extreme thorniness — it has far more prickles per inch than rugosa rose, swamp rose, or any of our other native roses.
Climbing prairie rose stands out from other New England roses primarily by its vigorous climbing habit with long, flexible canes.
Unlike New England's native roses such as swamp rose or Carolina rose which have green leaves, red-leaved rose's blue-gray to purplish foliage is unmistakable.
